content.title: The Role of Innovative Sectors in Future Energy Systems
content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations

content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

This lesson explores how emerging sectors are transforming the architecture of future energy systems through decentralization, digitization, and diversification.

It examines the rapid rise of distributed energy resources such as community solar and microgrids, and how these models are redefining energy access, resilience, and equity, particularly in developing countries.
The lesson presents the opportunity provided by peer-to-peer energy trading and blockchain applications, highlighting their potential to create localized energy markets and empower prosumers. It also investigates the growing role of energy cooperatives in democratizing energy access and driving community-led development.

In addition, the lesson presents advances in next-generation renewable technologies, including solar PV, wind, hybrid systems, and ocean energy, emphasizing their role in shaping cleaner, more adaptive energy futures.

By showcasing real-world innovations and development impacts, the lesson underscores how emerging sectors can enable inclusive, decentralized, and sustainable energy transitions.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Part 1: Distributed energy resources and decentralized grids

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: A: Growth of community solar and localized microgrids

content.text:
The evolution of community solar and localized microgrids is reshaping the global energy landscape, offering scalable, decentralized solutions that are particularly well suited to the needs of developing countries. Together, these innovations signal a shift toward more resilient, inclusive, and efficient energy systems that transform how power is produced, delivered, and shared.


Community solar, typically midsized solar arrays (500 kW to 10 MW), enables individuals, especially renters and those without rooftop access, to subscribe to a portion of a local solar project and receive utility bill credits. The next generation of community solar, known as Community Solar+, builds on this model by bundling clean energy generation with services like EV charging, energy storage, and backup power. A pilot in Vermont, USA, for example, added $1.1 million in value by integrating resilience and solar canopies (RMI, 2022). Meanwhile, community solar projects have saved low-income households $40–$50 per month and offered financing to over 70% of subscribers with low credit scores.

Localized microgrids, referring to small, self-contained energy systems that can operate with or without connection to the main grid, are another example of innovative distributed energy. By 2017, there were 1,869 microgrids worldwide totaling 20.7 GW of capacity, with projections of a fivefold increase in capacity and investment between 2018 and 2027, especially across Asia-Pacific (Uddin et al., 2023). Microgrids are proving invaluable in areas with weak or non-existent grid infrastructure, such as island communities, rural villages, mining operations, and refugee camps. They provide critical services with uninterrupted power through "island mode" operation, support renewable energy integration, and enhance power quality for sensitive sectors like healthcare and education.

For developing countries, these models offer an opportunity to leapfrog traditional grid expansion.

Community Solar+ can turn schools, health centers, and transit hubs into multi-functional energy hubs, powering services, creating local jobs, and strengthening resilience against climate shocks. Similarly, hybrid microgrids that combine solar, wind, batteries, and sometimes diesel or micro-hydro are increasingly viable for off-grid electrification, offering stable, low-carbon power at a manageable cost per kWh.

Beyond their technical capabilities, both community solar and microgrids are catalyzing new economic models and value streams. Across the board, distributed energy resources, if strategically deployed, could reduce system costs by up to $500 billion globally.

Looking ahead, these distributed solutions are foundational to achieving SDG 7 and enabling a just energy transition. They offer flexible, modular alternatives to centralized systems, especially important in the face of climate vulnerability and rising energy demand. To unlock their full potential in the Global South, governments and development actors must prioritize enabling policies, innovative financing, and inclusive design approaches that center community ownership and long-term resilience.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: B: Peer-to-peer energy trading and blockchain applications

content.text:
The rise of peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading, enabled by blockchain technology and smart contracts, will play a key role in the future of energy systems by decentralizing control, improving efficiency, and unlocking local energy markets. At its core, P2P trading allows prosumers (those who both produce and consume electricity) to directly exchange energy with consumers, bypassing traditional centralized intermediaries (Dong et al., 2025). Transactions occur within microgrids or distributed energy systems and are securely recorded on blockchain platforms, ensuring immutability, transparency, and traceability.


Blockchain-based P2P systems significantly reduce transaction costs and improve speed by eliminating middlemen. They also enhance grid resilience through localized demand response and load balancing, making energy systems more robust in the face of disruptions. Smart contracts, self-executing code embedded on the blockchain, contribute to automate the trading process. These contracts manage energy credits, incentivize consumption behavior through demand response mechanisms, and dynamically adjust pricing.


A key innovation is the use of dynamic pricing models that reflect real-time local energy conditions. Prices adjust based on a supply–demand ratio: when supply exceeds demand, prices fall to stimulate usage; when demand exceeds supply, prices rise to encourage generation. This flexibility improves the economic efficiency of decentralized systems and encourages greater investment in renewables. Simulations confirm the scalability and effectiveness of this approach, with test systems including a 500 kW solar array, a 550 kW load, and a 2500 kWh battery executing trades in real-time using Web3-enabled smart contracts.

For developing countries, these innovations can hold promise. In rural or off-grid areas where centralized infrastructure is lacking or unreliable, P2P trading can enable communities to trade locally generated solar power and achieve energy independence. Token-based incentives turn passive consumers into active participants, while smart meters and digital IDs ensure secure and inclusive access to energy markets.



By reducing reliance on long-distance transmission lines and increasing system redundancy, localized energy trading also supports climate adaptation and energy justice—especially during emergencies or peak demand periods.




Despite the potential, scaling P2P energy trading in developing contexts will require addressing key challenges. These include the absence of standardized regulatory frameworks, high upfront deployment costs, and the need for policy support to enable widespread adoption. But with the right investments and governance models, blockchain-enabled P2P trading could become a foundational pillar of inclusive, resilient, and low-carbon energy systems of the future.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: C: Role of energy cooperatives in democratizing energy access

content.text:
Energy cooperatives can help advance universal energy access in developing countries by offering a decentralized, people-centered solution to extend clean and affordable energy where it’s most urgently needed.


These cooperatives operate on principles of voluntary membership, democratic governance, benefit sharing, and local empowerment. By enabling residents to become both energy producers and consumers, cooperatives foster local ownership and build trust in renewable energy systems.

Their community-rooted approach has already scaled significantly in several countries, notably in Africa where electricity access is a priority:

content.body: In Uganda, Kyegegwa Rural Electricity Cooperative Society serves ~9,000 people connected to the national grid and a recently launched a solar minigrid to power 120 homes (NRECA International, 2023).

In Zambia, the Ntatumbila Power Electric Cooperative Society, reached 400 homes via solar mini-grid in 2024, thanks to a partnership with NRECA Internationa and the Zambia’s Rural Electrification Authority (Rural Electric Magazine, 2023). Electric cooperative also play a key role in electrification in other regions.
In the Philippines, approximately half of all households and the majority in rural areas, now rely upon electric cooperatives for power (Escresa et al., 2024).
In Bangladesh, local electric co-ops or PBS (Palli Bidyut Samities ) serve more than 100 million people across the country (NRECA International, 2023).

content.text:
Beyond expanding access, energy cooperatives generate tangible economic and social benefits.

They access funding through diverse sources including government loans, crowdfunding, and green energy certificates, and typically reinvest profits locally. A portion of revenue is often allocated to community development funds.

In Eastern Europe and the Western Balkans, citizen-led energy initiatives are gaining momentum.

content.body: For example, in Croatia, the city of Krizevci established the country’s first crowdfunded solar power plant through a cooperative model, which installed 30 kW of solar capacity on a public building (Wierling et al., 2018).
In Serbia, the Elektropionir cooperative initiated similar citizen-led projects, focusing on solar PV and building public engagement around energy transition.

content.text: These initiatives often combine community ownership with educational outreach, and while still modest in scale, they are creating replicable models that empower local actors and demonstrate the viability of decentralized renewable energy in traditionally utility-dominated markets.

Importantly, energy cooperatives also serve as platforms for inclusive and gender-responsive energy transitions. Through mechanisms like gender quotas, leadership training, and equitable access to dividends and employment, cooperatives ensure that women can play leading roles in the energy value chain. This is particularly impactful in remote and rural areas, where women often bear the brunt of energy poverty.

When it comes to financing, rural energy cooperatives adopt diverse financing and revenue strategies tailored to their local socioeconomic, geographic, and policy contexts, as displayed in the infographic. By blending local and external funding sources, they are able to provide affordable energy services while reinvesting in community development.

To fund renewable energy projects and maintain operations, cooperatives commonly use commercial loans, government-backed low- or no-interest loans, and issue equity or bonds. Power purchase agreements help secure long-term revenue and improve creditworthiness. Additional financing tools include membership fees, crowdfunding, and support from public credit agencies.

Government policies play a critical enabling role, offering preferential loans, tax incentives, and subsidies that reduce upfront costs and support infrastructure investment. These measures collectively lower financial barriers and foster the growth of community-led renewable energy systems.

Although challenges such as regulatory uncertainty, limited funding, and technical gaps persist, especially in developing regions, emerging digital tools like peer-to-peer trading, smart meters, and blockchain are enabling cooperatives to scale more efficiently and manage increasingly complex distributed systems.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Part 3: Advancements in next-generation of renewable energy

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: A: Advancement in Solar Energy

content.text:
As the global push for clean and affordable energy intensifies, solar PV technologies have become a key technology for the future of the energy transition. By early 2024, more than 1.6 terawatts (TW) of PV systems were operational worldwide, generating 2,135 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity, representing 8.3% of global electricity demand (IEA, 2024). In 2023 alone, a record 456 gigawatts (GW) of new PV capacity was installed, with China (277 GW) leading the way.


Much of this success stems from rapid advancements in solar technologies.

Today, monocrystalline silicon (c-Si) modules dominate the market, representing 98% of global cell production and achieving module efficiencies of 20%–25% (IEA, 2024). In parallel, thin-film technologies, such as cadmium telluride (CdTe) and copper indium gallium diselenide (CIGS), have reached module efficiencies nearing 20%, offering benefits in lower material use and manufacturing costs.

Another notable innovation are perovskite-based tandem cells. They are advanced solar technologies that layer a perovskite material on top of traditional silicon cells to capture more sunlight and achieve higher efficiency than conventional solar cells. They are emerging as the fastest-evolving solar innovation, with lab-tested efficiencies of up to 33.9%. Commercial deployment has already begun in several markets, with Chinese manufacturers shipping perovskite modules in 2022 and 2023.

Other configurations like bifacial modules, which harvest light from both sides of the panel, represented about 50% of all PV installations in 2023. When combined with single-axis tracking, these systems can boost energy yields by 30–35% compared to fixed installations (IEA, 2024). Additional innovations such as floating PV systems and agrivoltaics are helping to address land scarcity in dense or rural areas, offering co-benefits such as reduced evaporation, better module cooling, and improved agricultural productivity.


These advancements are promising for energy access in developing countries. Small-scale applications like solar home systems (SHS) and pico-PV systems, small-scale photovoltaic systems typically under 10 watts, are already providing essential services such as lighting and phone charging to millions without grid access.

Moreover, hybrid PV-diesel mini-grids with battery storage are being deployed to deliver more reliable and cost-effective electricity in remote areas, reducing diesel dependence and improving service quality. The growing deployment of PV-integrated infrastructure, from building facades to irrigation systems, is the sign of a broader shift toward decentralized, multifunctional energy solutions tailored to local development needs.


Economically, the solar sector has become a major driver of green growth. By 2023, it supported 7 million jobs globally and had an estimated market value of USD 400 billion (IEA, 2024).

By 2050, the industry is expected to create over 22.2 million jobs in the energy sector by 2050.


As installation costs plummet, utility-scale PV is now 25–50% cheaper than concentrated solar power (CSP), and often competitive with gas generation, the case for scaling solar in developing regions grows stronger. However, continued progress will require not just technological innovation, but also streamlined permitting, improved grid infrastructure, and fair pricing systems to ensure inclusive benefits across all segments of society.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: B: Advancement in Wind Energy

content.text:
wind energy will also play a defining role in the future of global energy systems, with next-generation technologies offering both scale and opportunity for sustainable development. In 2024, a record 117 GW of wind capacity was installed worldwide, bringing the global total to 1,136 GW (GWEC, 2025). Wind accounted for 20% of all new power additions, part of the 90% share captured by renewables overall. This momentum is expected to accelerate, with annual wind additions projected to average 164 GW per year from 2025 to 2030, totaling nearly 981 GW in that period.

Together, wind and solar are expected to provide 30% of global electricity by 2030, double their share today.


Offshore wind is at the forefront of this expansion, with over 380 GW projected to be installed globally by 2034 (WEF, 2024). The European Union leads with a target of 300 GW by 2050 under initiatives like the North Sea Energy Cooperation (NSEC). However, a drop in new offshore installations from 11 GW in 2023 to 8 GW in 2024 signals the urgent need for policy continuity and investment support to realize this potential.


The future of wind energy is also increasingly shaped by developing countries. In 2024, Africa and the Middle East doubled their onshore wind additions, with rising capacity in Uzbekistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and South Africa.

Despite these advances, high financing costs driven by perceived investment risks remain a barrier. Yet the wind sector is raising significant capital, attracting over USD 200 billion in private investment annually and already supporting 1.5 million jobs worldwide, highlighting its potential as a development engine if de-risked effectively (GWEC, 2025).

Globally, wind energy is shifting the geopolitical landscape. China alone accounted for 70% of new installations in 2024, reducing its dependency on imported oil while positioning itself as a leader in renewable manufacturing and deployment.


Yet, wind energy’s growth faces persistent constraints. More than 1,650 GW of renewable capacity, including wind, is in advanced development but waiting for grid connections. Supply chains are stretched, onshore turbine manufacturing capacity stands at 145 GW, barely matching 2030 demand, while offshore capacity lags even further (IEA, 2024). Wind projects are also hindered by permitting delays, grid congestion, and disinformation campaigns that erode public trust.


To overcome these barriers, investment in grid infrastructure, storage solutions, and permitting reform is essential. Technological advancements, particularly in next-generation offshore turbines, that are larger, more powerful wind turbines designed for greater efficiency in deep-sea environments, and R&D initiatives aim to enhance performance and reduce costs.

At the same time, aligning wind energy with national industrialization, job creation, and energy access strategies will be key to maximizing its role in sustainable development.

In short, next-generation wind energy can be a lever for energy equity, economic resilience, and global stability for a just energy transition.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: C: Hybrid Renewable energy systems

content.text:
As the global energy transition accelerates, the future of electrification will be shaped by how smartly and sustainably we generate and distribute it. Between 2010 and 2020, global renewable energy capacity more than doubled, from 1,240 TWh to 2,960 TWh, driven by falling costs, policy support, and climate imperatives. In this evolving landscape, hybrid renewable energy systems (HRES) are emerging as a cornerstone of resilient, reliable, and equitable electrification (Hassan et al., 2023).


HRES combine two or more renewable sources, most often solar and wind, with integrated storage technologies to overcome the intermittency challenges of single-source systems. By leveraging complementary generation profiles, such as solar peaking during the day and wind often stronger at night, HRES ensure a more continuous energy supply. Storage solutions like batteries, supercapacitors, and pumped hydro allow surplus energy to be stored and released when needed, reducing curtailment and increasing system efficiency.


This innovation is technical, but also has vast development implications. HRES are especially valuable in off-grid and remote areas, where traditional grid expansion is costly or impractical.

Microgrids built with hybrid systems are increasingly deployed in rural regions, offering sustainable alternatives to diesel generators and enhancing local energy independence. In Al Minya, Egypt, for instance, a solar PV and battery system achieved a remarkably low energy cost of $0.059/kWh, showing that clean off-grid power can also be cost-competitive (Rezk et al., 2019).

Hybrid systems are also versatile. On-grid configurations support national grids through net metering and improved voltage stability, while off-grid and microgrid systems can power schools, health clinics, farms, and entire communities autonomously. In Shanghai, optimized PV-battery systems demonstrated lower energy costs that approach grid parity, which is the point at which the cost of renewable energy becomes equal to or less than the cost of electricity from conventional sources on the grid, without subsidies.

As electrification extends to new regions, smart hybrid systems will play a vital role in shaping energy access that is not only cleaner, but also more resilient and inclusive. When optimized using tools like machine learning and maximum power point tracking (MPPT), hybrid systems can adapt to weather patterns and load fluctuations. In Iran, for example, a hybrid system combining 1 kW of PV, two 3 kW wind turbines, and a diesel backup achieved a levelized cost of $0.462/kWh, showing that even in challenging environments, hybrid solutions can deliver reliable energy (Hassan et al., 2023).

However, scale-up must be mindful of sustainability. In small-scale systems, a significant part of the environmental impact can come from battery storage, which highlights the need for responsible lifecycle management and innovation in storage technologies. But the gains from storage are substantial: a grid-connected hybrid PV-battery system can reduce net present cost by 15.6% and energy costs by 16.8% compared to fossil-based alternatives.


In the future, electrification will be more decentralized, data-driven, and modular. Hybrid renewable energy systems will help contribute to building a new model of electrification that is clean, adaptive, and tailored to local needs.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: D: Ocean Energy

content.text:
In the future, electrification will be more decentralized, resilient, and tailored to local needs. Ocean energy, drawing from wave, tidal, thermal, and salinity gradient resources, will play a growing role in this transformation.

As a predictable and locally available renewable resource, ocean energy can be well-suited to the electrification of remote and coastal communities. With global trends moving toward diversified energy systems, the unique attributes of ocean energy offer opportunities to power not just households, but entire sectors of the blue economy, including aquaculture, water desalination, and marine data platforms.


The global market potential for ocean energy stands at 350 gigawatts by 2050 (IRENA, 2023),

Ocean energy can provide clean, local and predictable electricity to coastal countries and island communities around the world .

In China, for instance, tidal and wave projects in the Zhoushan and Zhejiang islands demonstrate scalable innovation, with the Wanshan 1 MW wave energy project already deployed at sea (Dai et al., 2023). These developments highlight both the growing viability of marine energy and the engineering challenges ahead, such as device survivability under extreme conditions like typhoons.

ocean thermal energy conversion (OTEC) also holds promise.

In India’s Lakshadweep islands, low-temperature thermal desalination (LTTD) plants have been delivering clean water since 2005, each producing 100 m³/day for populations of around 10,000 (PIB, 2022). Future plants aim to run entirely on OTEC, reducing diesel dependence and enhancing sustainability in fragile island ecosystems.

Salinity gradient power, another underutilized resource, offers a global technical potential of 647 GW (IRENA, 2014). This technology refers to the electricity generated from the natural pressure or electrochemical potential created when freshwater and seawater mix across specialized membranes. Although no major river delta has yet been exploited, over 140 rivers worldwide discharge more than 2,000 m³/s, which could be a vast untapped opportunity particularly in coastal areas of the Global South.

Ocean energy can also align strongly with development goals.

In Cape Verde, where desalination meets 85% of water needs and renewable water availability is just 537 m³/person/year (well below the 1,700 m³/person/year standard), wave-powered desalination could enhance water security while avoiding fossil fuel use.

content.body: Ocean energy systems face higher upfront costs and limited deployment infrastructure, particularly in isolated or weather-exposed regions.
Policy frameworks are often underdeveloped, though countries like China are beginning to integrate ocean energy into national strategies.
Technological hurdles such as membrane efficiency (for salinity gradient systems) and device durability require further innovation and investment.

content.text: Despite its significant potential, ocean energy still faces critical barriers that must be addressed to enable wider adoption and long-term viability:

As electrification evolves, ocean energy offers a compelling addition to the future energy mix, especially for communities on the frontlines of climate change and development challenges. With supportive policies and sustained R&D, it can help deliver clean, reliable, and context-appropriate power across the globe.

content.title: Key Takeaways
content.intro: If you only have space to remember 3 things:

takeaways.title: Distributed energy systems are foundational to the future of energy. Emerging models like community solar, microgrids, and hybrid renewable systems offer scalable, resilient solutions tailored to local needs. These decentralized approaches not only expand access but also empower communities, reduce costs, and enhance energy security.

Digital innovation is unlocking new energy markets and participation. Technologies like blockchain and peer-to-peer trading are reshaping how energy is produced, exchanged, and valued. By enabling local energy transactions, automating smart contracts, and incentivizing prosumer engagement, these tools are making energy systems more inclusive, efficient, and adaptable.

Emerging technologies and sectors are diversifying the global energy mix. From next-generation solar and wind to ocean energy and energy cooperatives, new technologies and institutional models are driving a more sustainable and equitable energy transition. Their success depends not just on innovation, but on supportive policies, financing mechanisms, and community-centered design.
